subject: physics
title: Electromagnetism and solenoids
key_idea: A current in a wire produces a magnetic field around it, stronger with more current and nearer the wire. Coiling the wire into a solenoid makes the field stronger. An iron core makes an electromagnet that can be switched on and off.

sections.heading: The magnetic field around a wire

blocks.text: A current in a wire produces a magnetic field around the wire. This is the magnetic effect of a current.

items: The field forms circles around the wire.
The strength of the field depends on the current and on the distance from the wire.
A bigger current gives a stronger field. The field is weaker further from the wire.
Reversing the current reverses the direction of the field.
Switch the current on and off near a plotting compass. The needle moves when the current is on.
Move the compass around the wire. The direction of the needle changes.
Pass the wire through a card, sprinkle iron filings on it and switch on the current. The filings form circles.
A current produces a magnetic field around a wire.
The field is stronger with a bigger current and closer to the wire.

blocks.text: A solenoid is a coil of wire. Coiling the wire makes the magnetic field much stronger than that of a straight wire.

items.meaning: A wire shaped into a coil.
A solenoid with an iron core. It is a magnet that can be switched on and off.

items: The field inside a solenoid is strong and uniform.
The field outside has a similar shape to the field of a bar magnet.
Adding an iron core makes the field stronger.

blocks.text: Pick a change to the electromagnet to see its effect.

diagram.alt: Pick a change to a solenoid and see the effect on the strength and direction of its magnetic field.

options.label: Increase the current
options.explanation: A bigger current gives a stronger field.

options.label: Decrease the current
options.explanation: A smaller current gives a weaker field.

options.label: Add more turns of wire
options.explanation: More turns increase the magnetic effect.

options.label: Wind the coil the opposite way
Move the electromagnet further from the iron
options.explanation: The field is weaker further from the coil.

items: A solenoid has a stronger field than a straight wire.
The field is stronger with more current, more turns or an iron core.
An electromagnet is a solenoid with an iron core.

blocks.text: You can measure the strength of an electromagnet by counting the paper clips it picks up. Change one variable at a time.

items: Change the number of turns and keep the current the same. Keep the core, the paper clips and the distance the same.
To test the current, keep the number of turns constant and change the current several times.
More turns pick up more paper clips. The number of clips can be directly proportional to the number of turns.
It can be switched on and off, so it is easy to demagnetise.
It picks up and releases magnetic materials, as in a crane for moving iron and steel.
A bigger current and a closer electromagnet increase the force on a piece of iron or steel.
Change only one variable at a time.
An electromagnet can be switched off, so the metal it picks up is easy to release.

checks.q: Describe how a teacher can use a plotting compass to demonstrate the magnetic effect of the current in a wire.
checks.a: Switch the current on and off, which makes the compass needle move. Or move the compass around the wire, which changes the direction of the needle.

checks.q: Give two ways the magnetic field around a coil could be made stronger.
checks.a: Any two from: increase the current, insert an iron core, increase the number of turns.

checks.q: Explain one reason why an electromagnet is used instead of a permanent magnet to separate iron and steel from other metals.
checks.a: It can be switched off (it is easy to demagnetise), so it is easy to remove the separated metal.

blocks.text: Separate science students must explain how devices work from diagrams. In an electric bell, an electromagnet pulls an iron arm towards it.

items.text: There is a current in the circuit.
A magnetic field is created around the electromagnet.
A resultant force acts on the iron arm, causing it to move towards the electromagnet.
The iron arm returns to its original position.

worked_example.question:
A magnet produces a magnetic field. A toy crane uses an electromagnet to pick up and move blocks.

Explain how this electromagnet is able to pick up and move the blocks.
answer_points: Completing the circuit turns the electromagnet on.
There is a current in the coil.
A magnetic field is produced around the coil.
The iron core becomes magnetised.
Move the electromagnet towards the blocks: the block is attracted to the electromagnet.
Moving the crane moves the block.
Switching off the current switches off the electromagnet, releasing the block.
worked_example.tip: A level of response question: link the points in a logical order from switching on to releasing the block.

worked_example.question:
A student has
− a power pack
− a long piece of wire
− a stiff card
− iron filings

Describe how the student could use this equipment to show the shape of the magnetic field produced by a current in the wire.

You may draw a diagram to help with your answer.
answer_points: Put the wire through the card (or near, under or over the card).
Put iron filings on the card or around the wire.
Connect the wire to the power pack.
Switch on, so there is a current in the wire.
The filings are attracted or move.
A pattern is seen in the filings: circles around the wire.
worked_example.tip: Any four points score. Marks can be taken from a diagram.

extra.heading: Direction of the field and the field of a solenoid

blocks.text: The direction of the field depends on the direction of the current. The right-hand grip rule gives it.

items: Point the thumb of the right hand along the current in a straight wire. The fingers curl in the direction of the field.
Inside a solenoid the fields from the individual coils add together. This makes a very strong, almost uniform field along the centre.
Outside the solenoid the fields cancel. This gives a weaker field.

worked_example.question:
A teacher sets up equipment to demonstrate using a plotting compass to investigate the magnetic field around a current-carrying wire. The equipment is a current-carrying wire, a wooden stand, a cardboard sheet and a plotting compass.

Describe how the teacher uses this equipment to show the shape of the magnetic field around the current-carrying wire.
answer_points: Place the plotting compass onto the cardboard sheet.
Mark the direction of the compass needle (with a dot).
Move the plotting compass to another of these marks and repeat.
Connect the marks together to show the field.
worked_example.tip: Any three points score. One mark is given for using the plotting compass to show the field if nothing else scores.

worked_example.question:
A solid bar is inside a copper solenoid. The solenoid is connected in series with a battery and a variable resistor. The device is an electromagnet.
The resistance of the variable resistor increases.
Explain what happens to the magnetic field surrounding the bar and state how the pattern of field lines that represents the field changes.
answer_points: The current in the coil decreases.
Because the current decreases, the magnetic field strength decreases.
Because the field is weaker, there are fewer field lines in the same area, or the field lines are further apart.
worked_example.tip: Link each step to the one before: resistance, then current, then field strength, then spacing of the lines.

items: The field lines around a straight wire are circles that get further apart away from the wire, so the field is weaker there.

Right-hand grip rule: point the thumb along the current and the curled fingers show the direction of the field lines. For a solenoid, curl the fingers the way the current goes round and the thumb points to the north end.
Permanent magnets are used in fridge catches, loudspeakers and compasses.
Electromagnets are used in cranes, locks, bells and relays.
A loudspeaker uses a changing current in a coil next to a permanent magnet to move a cone and make sound.

items.text: A small current in the first circuit flows through the coil of an electromagnet.
The electromagnet attracts a soft iron armature.
The armature moves and closes the contacts of a second circuit, which switches on a larger current.

blocks.text: A relay lets a small current in a safe circuit switch a larger current, such as a mains motor.

worked_example.question:
Describe the construction of a simple electromagnet that is producing a magnetic field.
You may draw a diagram to help your answer.
answer_points: A solenoid or coil of wire.
A (direct) current in the wire, coil or solenoid.
A (soft) iron core.
worked_example.tip: Labels on a diagram can score all three marks.

items: An electromagnet is a coil of wire with a current in it, wound round a core of **soft iron**.
Soft iron is used because it magnetises and demagnetises easily.

blocks.text: The field of a flat circular coil

items: Near each part of the wire, the field lines are circles around the wire.
Through the middle of the coil, the field lines pass in the same direction, and the field is strongest there.
Reversing the current reverses the direction of the field.

Right-hand grip rule: point the thumb along the current and the curled fingers show the direction of the field lines. For a solenoid, curl the fingers the way the current goes round and the thumb points to the north end.
